title: Minimum Number of Removals to Make Mountain Array
statement:
An array `arr` is a **mountain** when it has at least 3 elements and some peak index `i` with `0 < i < arr.length - 1` such that the values rise strictly from `arr[0]` up to `arr[i]` and then fall strictly from `arr[i]` down to `arr[arr.length - 1]`.

You may delete any elements of `nums` (the rest keep their relative order). Return the fewest deletions that turn `nums` into a mountain. The input always allows at least one way to do it.
constraints: nums can always be turned into a mountain by deleting elements
notes:
## Intuition

Deleting as few elements as possible means keeping as many as possible, so look for the longest subsequence that is a mountain. Fix the peak at index `i`: the part before it is a strictly increasing subsequence ending at `i`, and the part after it is a strictly decreasing subsequence starting at `i`. The two choices are independent, so the best mountain with peak `i` has length `up[i] + down[i] - 1` (the peak is counted twice).

Both quantities are longest-increasing-subsequence lengths: `up` reads `nums` left to right, and `down` is the same computation on the reversed array, reversed back. Trying every subset would be exponential; even the plain LIS DP is O(n²), while the "tails" method with binary search gives O(n log n).

## Approach

1. `risingLengths(values)` returns, for each position, the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence ending there. `tails[k]` holds the smallest possible last value of a rising run of length `k + 1`; binary search finds the first tail `>= value`, `value` replaces it, and the run length is `left + 1`.
2. `up = risingLengths(nums)`, `down = risingLengths(reversed nums)` reversed back.
3. For every inner index `i`, a peak needs at least one smaller element on each side: `up[i] > 1` and `down[i] > 1`. Keep the largest `up[i] + down[i] - 1` in `longest`.
4. Return `n - longest`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,3,1]`. Left to right, `up = [1, 2, 1]` (the second `1` is not larger than `1`, so it replaces the first tail). On the reversed array `[1,3,1]` the lengths are `[1, 2, 1]`, so `down = [1, 2, 1]`. Only `i = 1` is inner, with `up[1] = down[1] = 2`, giving `longest = 2 + 2 - 1 = 3`. The answer is `3 - 3 = 0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): each element does one binary search in each direction.
- Space: O(n) for `up`, `down` and `tails`.

## Pitfalls

- Require `up[i] > 1` and `down[i] > 1`: a peak at the very first or last kept element is not a mountain.
- The rise and fall must be strict, so the binary search looks for the first tail `>= value`, not `> value`.
- Do not subtract the peak twice: the mountain length is `up[i] + down[i] - 1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tails` | `tails[k]`: smallest last value of a strictly rising run of length `k + 1` |
| `lengths` | rising-run length ending at each position |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary search bounds over `tails` |
| `up`, `down` | longest strict rise ending at `i` / strict fall starting at `i` |
| `longest` | length of the longest mountain subsequence found |
